The Petitioner/workman filed an application before this Tribunal under section 2A (2) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as “I.D.Act”) dated 21-02-2018.. 


The fact of the case, in brief is that the petitioner was engaged as a cleaning staff on daily wage basis at the 
office of the Railway Recruitment Cell, Eastern Railway, Kolkata from 01-05-2010. He was entrusted with the work 
of cleaning the entire office premises of the railway authority at 56, C.R. Avenue, Kolkata. 


The proposal for engagement as labour on contract basis at a daily wage far below the minimum wages 
approved by the Ministry of Labour, Central Govt. for employment of sweeping and cleaning staff. The 
petitioner/workman was initially paid Rs.84.02 per day. After rendering services for seven years the Chief 
O.S./Recruitment put up a note dated 12-02-2013 for revision of wages of the daily waged labourer who were 
performing cleaning job in the office premises. The proposal for enhancing the wages was at the rate of Rs.217/- per 
day including a bonus @ Rs.36.15 per day but the employer authority enhanced the daily wages to Rsd.150/- per day. 


The Petitioner served at the office of the Railway Recruitment Cell, Eastern Railway without any break. It 
has further stated that there was no provision for any leave and they had to work even on holidays and Sundays. The 
employer authority did not pay the minimum wages and the petitioner made several representations to the office of 
the Railway Recruitment Cell, which went unheard. Subsequently, the petitioner made a presentation before the 
authority under Minimum Wages Act, 1948 alleging non-payment of minimum wages. 


The Chairman, Railway Recruitment Cell was not pleased with the action of the petitioner/workman. 
Consequently, the petitioner was terminated from his service without issuing any letter of termination. Accordingly to 
the petitioner he had been performing work continuously and the employer authority terminated him illegally without 
complying the due process of law. 


On being aggrieved with the illegal termination a complaint was submitted before the Regional Labour 
Commissioner- “Central” at Kolkata on 05-09-2017. The Conciliation proceeding failed and the petitioner filed this 
application before this Tribunal u/s 2A(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act challenging the illegal termination. The 
petitioner has prayed for setting aside the illegal termination, for reinstatement, payment of back wages and payment 
of retrenchment compensation u/s 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act along with consequently relief. 


The Chairman, Railway Recruitment Cell, Eastern Railway along with another contested the case by filing 
written statement on 20-07-2018. Admittedly the petitioner was deployed under the Respondent Authority on daily 
wage labourer on the basis of ‘no work no pay’ . According to the Respondent discontinuation of service of the 
workman was not in violation of any existing rules or principle of natural justice. It is contended that the petitioner 
has no legal right to enter the premises of the Railway without sanction from the concerned authority. The 
Respondent asserted that the workman was terminated from the service of Railway Recruitment Cell of the Railway 
and notice had been tendered but the workman refused to acknowledge receipt of the same. It is contended that there 
was no scope for seeking explanation or initiating any disciplinary proceeding against the petitioner for the purpose of 
discontinuing his work as his engagement was on day to day basis. The employer asserted that the petitioner is not 
entitled to reinstatement in service and he is also not entitled to any payment of back wages or retrenchment 
compensation under section 25-F of the I. D. Act. The Respondent urged the application is liable to be dismissed. 


Points for Consideration: 


On the basis of the statement of claim and the written objection filed by the Respondent, following issues are 
framed for determination : 


1. Whether the application u/s 2A (2) of the Industrial Disputes Act is maintainable? 


2. Whether the petitioner/workman is entitled to retrenchment compensation or reinstatement in his service 
along with back wages? 


In order to prove his case Sri Dipankar Halder examined himself as Workman Witness No.1. He filed an Affidavit in 
Chief reiterating the case disclosed in his application. In his affidavit in chief the workman further stated that he was 
working in the premises of the Railway Recruitment Cell, Eastern Railway, Kolkata as a daily rated worker w.e.f. 01- 
05-2012. The Respondent company paid him Rs.,84.02 per day as safaiwala which is far below the minimum wages. 
A proposal was put up on 12-02-2013 for revision of wages of the contractual workers who were doing cleaning job 
in the office premises for payment of Rs.217/- per day but the Respondent Authority increased the wages only to 
Rs.150/-. It is further stated that his office was open on all days of the work including Sundays and there was no leave 
facility. The workman disclosed that he made a representation before the authority under the Minimum Wages Act, 
1948 alleging non-payment of minimum wages. 


The Respondent company was annoyed with him and his work was terminated from 31-08-2017. He was not

2. A copy of joint petition submitted by Sri Suman Das and one Sri Dipankar Halder before Railway Authority

3. Copies of letters issued by Railway dated 01-08-2016 is marked as Exb.W-3 and W-3/A. 
4. Copy of petition addressed Regional Labour Commissioner as Exb.W-4. 


5. Copy of certificate issued by Regional Labour Commissioner u/s 2A of the Industrial Dispute Act dated 30- 
10-2017 as Exb.W-5. 


6. Copy of note sheet dated 18-05-2006 relating to recruitment of sanitation workers in RRC is collectively 
marked as Exb.-W-6. 


7. Copy of payment sheet for the month of March, 2015 as Exb.W-7. 


8. Copy of order passed by R.L.C under Minimum Wages Act dated 16-10-2017 is collectively marked as 
Exb.W-8. 


In course of cross examination the witness admitted that he worked as daily wage labourer at ‘no work no pay’ 
basis. Apart from Safaiwala’s job he performed other office works also, but did not mention what other works he used 
to perform. The workman also admitted that as per order of the Labour Commissioner compensation was paid to him 
on three occasions before hearing of the Minimum Wages Act. 


The management of the Respondent establishment examined Smt. Sucharita Das, Management Witness No.1. She 
filed an affidavit in chief where she stated that the petitioner was assigned with cleaning job on daily wage basis and 
there was no assurance for his regularization in the job. The witness denied the allegation of the petitioner relating to 
illegal termination from his employment. The witness further averred that by discontinuation of his service the 
authority did not violate any existing rule and that the service of the petitioner was terminated in accordance with the 
law. The witness further stated that after hearing the claim application, the authority under the Minimum Wages Act 
allowed three compensations in respect of the arrear of differential wages amounting to Rs.5,68,284/- in favour of the 
petitioner and the same has already been paid by the Railway Authority. It is stated that the application filed by the 
petitioner is liable to be dismissed. In the course of her examination in chief, the witness produced a copy of order 
dated 16-10-2017 passed by the authority under the Minimum Wages Act relating to payment of minimum wages 
which has been marked as Exb.M-1. 


In cross examination the management witness deposed that she had no personal knowledge about the employment of 
the workman. She also deposed she has no knowledge since when the workman was employed as casual “Safai 
worker” by the Recruitment Cell. The management witness was unable to state if the service of the petitioner was 
continuous one or not. Regarding refusal of the workman to sign the letter of termination, the witness deposed that the 
workman did not refuse to sign the letter of termination in her presence and admitted that they have not produced 
letter of termination which hade been refused by the workman. 


Mr. Somnath Chakraborty, Ld. Advocate for the workman advancing his argument submitted that Sri Dipankar 
Halder was engaged as a daily wager under Railway Recruitment Cell of Eastern Railway at Kolkata on the basis of 
his letter of engagement which has been produced as Exb.W-3. The workman served continuously as a cleaning staff 
from 01-05-2012 till 31-08-2017. The workman was illegally terminated from his service of the Respondent without 
issuing any notice of termination or retrenchment. It is further argued that the workman was engaged at a daily wage 
of Rs.84.0[2 per day. The same was revised to Rs.150/- per day w.e.f. 12-02-2013 which was also less than the 
minimum wages to which the workman was entitled to at the relevant period. The workman made a representation 
before the authority under the Minimum Wages Act which was considered and an order was passed on 16-10-2017 
directing the O.P employer i.e. Railway Administration, Eastern Railway, Kolkata to deposit Rs.5,68,284/- in favour 
of Sri Suman Das within a period of 30 days as differential wages and a compensation three times the arrear of wages. 


The Ld. Advocated argued that the employer authority was annoyed with the claim of the workman for which he has 
been illegally terminated. It is urged that the workman has rendered continuous service to the Respondent as per 
section 25-B of the Industrial Disputes Act and he is entitled to retrenchment compensation under section 25-F of the 
Act for not issuing one month’s notice indicating the reason of the retrenchment. Ld. Advocate submitted that the 
workman may be paid his back wages and his service under Respondent may be restored. 


Mr. Abhijit Bhadra, Ld. Advocate for the Respondent refuting the claim argued that the workman was employed as 
a daily wager on the basis of ‘no work no pay’ and the workman is not entitled to any retrenchment compensation as

he has failed to prove that he rendered continuous service for at least 240 days in the preceding years. It has urged that 
the workman has already been paid his compensation and arrear wages up to 31-08-2017 and the instant application is 
liable to be dismissed with cost. 


Considered the rival arguments and written notes of argument in the light of the pleadings of the parties, evidence 
adduced and the law involved. Both the issues are taken up together for convenience of discussion. It is appeared to 
me that this is a case where the employee has been discontinued from his service and he made a complaint before the 
Regional Labour Commissioner (Central), Kolkata u/s 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act. The same resulted in failure 
and the certificate was issued by the Conciliation Officer u/s 2A of the Act on 30-10-2017. This application u/s 2A (2) 
has been filed before this Tribunal on 21-02-2018 which is within the statutory period of three years from the date of 
discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination of service. Therefore I hold that the case is maintainable. 


Admitted Sri Dipankar Halder was engaged as Safaiwala at the Railway Recruitment Cell of Eastern Railway, 
Kolkata from 01-05-2012. No formal letter of engagement has been produced by any of the parties. Ld. Advocate for 
the workman advancing his argument submitted that Exb.W-3, a letter dated 01-08-2016 is the letter of engagement 
of the workman. On a close reading of the same I find that Exb.W-3 is a reply to the claim made by the workman for 
regularization of the workman in his employment. From the said document it is gathered that the cleaning staff was 
engaged purely on daily wage basis without any assurance for regularization. In the application u/s 2A of I.D. Act 
seeking the restoration of service and payment of back wages. For the first time it is stated in paragraph 21(f) of the 
petition that the workman worked continuously for more than five years and is eligible for retrenchment 
compensation u/s 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act. The workman neither pleaded in his application as to how many 
days he had worked in the preceding years nor did he specify the number of days he was employed in each year since 
01-05-2010. No evidence has been adduced by him to prove that he has rendered continuous service to the respondent 
establishment as necessary u/s 25-B of the Industrial Disputes Act i.e. for not less than 240 days in a year. 


Ld. Advocate for the petitioner relying upon the order passed by the Authority under Minimum Wages Act (Exb.- 
W-9 collectively) submitted that while computing the arrears of differential wages paid to the workman, the entire 
period was accepted by the authority. Therefore it would be presumed that workman has rendered continuous service 
during the entire period of the previous years and he is entitled to retrenchment compensation which is equivalent to 
fifteen days’ average pay for every complete year of continuous service or any part thereof. 


On perusal of the order dated 16-10-2017 regarding payment of differential wages I find that there is no clear 
observation as to the total number of days of service rendered by the workman. It is simply stated that the O.P. 
employer/Railway Administration did not contest the minimum rate of wages and the period of work as claimed by 
the applicant in the instant claim application. I, therefore, hold that the said order passed by the authority under the 
Minimum Wages Act cannot substitute the burden of proof which lies upon the workman to establish that he has 
rendered continuous service for not less than 240 days in a calendar year during his said period of engagement. 


In the case of Essen Dinki —vs- Rajiv Kumar, 2002 III CLR 943, Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that the burden 
of proof that he was working for 240 days was upon the employee. There is no iota of evidence in this case to prove 
that the workman as a daily wage labourer had been engaged and rendered service for at least 240 days in a year 
under the employer. Accordingly I hold that the workman has failed to establish that he has fulfilled the condition 
precedence for application of the provision of section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act for payment of retrenchment 
compensation for the years of continuous service rendered. 


In this connection it is necessary to set out the relevant provisions which defines the term “retrenchment” in I.D. 
Act. Section 2(00) lays down : 


“retrenchment” means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, 
otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not include— 


(a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or 


(b) retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between 
the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf; or 


[(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of employment 
between the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract being terminated under a 
stipulation in that behalf contained therein; or] 


(c) termination of he service of a workman on the ground of continued ill-health]. 


In the instant case the workman, a daily wager has failed to discharge his burden that he has served continuously for 
at least 240 days in any one calendar year under the employer. Therefore, section 25-F of I.D. Act which lays down 
the condition precedence the retrenchment of workman would have no application. 


The workman therefore is not entitled to retrenchment compensation u/s 25-F (b) which is equivalent to 15 days’ 
average pay for every complete year of continuous service or any part there in excess of six months.

It emerges from evidence on record that the workman had lodged a complaint before the authority under Minimum 
Wages Act and on the basis of an order passed by the concerned authority on 16-10-2017 (Exb.W-9) the workman 
received differential minimum wages for the period of work along with compensation which was three times the 
wages which had fallen due. 


In the case of Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited —vs- Bhurumal; (2014) 7 SCC 177, the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
held as follows : 


“33... it is clear from the reading of the aforesaid judgments that the ordinary principle of grant of retrenchment 
with full back wages , when the termination is found to be illegal is not applied mechanically in all cases. While that 
may be the position where service of a regular/permanent worker are terminated illegally and/or malafide and/or by 
way of victimisation, unfair labour practice, etc. However, when it come to the case of termination of a daily-wage 
worker and where the termination is found illegal because of procedural defect namely in violation of section 25-F of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, this court is consistent in taking the view that in such cases reinstatement with back wages 
is not automatic and instead of the workman should be given monetary compensation which will meet the ends of 
justice...” 


employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be 
retrenched by that employer until - 


(a) 116 workman has been given one month’s notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and 
the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period 
of the notice. 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to 
fifteen days’ average pay (for every completed year of continuous service) or any part thereof in excess of 
six months. 


Therefore, the condition president to retrenchment of the workman u/s 25-F have not been fulfilled and the 
workman, a daily wage labourer is not entitled to one month’s prior notice in writing before his termination as 
provided u/s 25-F of the I.D. Act. 


Admitted the daily wager “cleaning staff’ of the respondent worked for several years and has been 
retrenched from his work without any notice. The engagement of the workman was not against any sanctioned post 
nor did he undergo any selection procedure before engagement. The workman has been discontinued from work since 
01-09-2017 and eight years have passed thereafter. The petitioner therefore has no legal right to be reinstated in his 
earlier place of work. He has received compensation on the basis of order passed in Exb.W-9 by the RPFC. The 
workman expected that he would continue to be employed by the respondent until his work was stopped abruptly. 
There is no evidence on record that he is gainfully employed at any other place since his termination. 


Therefore, applying the ratio of the decision posited in the case of Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. -vs- Bhurumal 
(supra), I hold that it would be just and appropriate to grant a monetary compensation to the workman for the unfair 
labour practice and his illegal termination without prior notice, which shall be equivalent to one month’s daily wage 
at the then prevailing rate. 


This issue noi.2 relating to relief is accordingly allowed in favour of the workman. 
The Industrial Dispute is allowed in part in favour of the workman. 
Hence, 

ORODERED 


that the Industrial Dispute u/s 2A (2) of the Industrial Disputes Act is allowed in part on contest against the 
respondent. The petitioner is granted monetary compensation equivalent to one month’s daily wages at the then 
prevailing rate. The amount shall be paid by the respondent within one month from date of communication of the 
award. Let the award be drawn in the light of my above discussion. Let the copies of the award, in duplicate be sent to 
the Ministry for information and notification.

1. Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against her termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along 
with continuity of service and full back wages. 


2. It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that she was appointed as sweeper/safai 
karamchari on 01.04.2017 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But 
the said minimum wages were never paid to her. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 1.75% 
ESI and Rs.300/- as TDS from his salary despite of the fact that her total wages comes under the ambit of tax 
free limit. She was working under respondent no.1 directly, but respondent 10.1 in order to avoid its liability 
always shows his employment in record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour 
practice. 


3. It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent no.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent 10.1. However, their demand was not 
accepted. Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently her services were 
dispensed with w.e.f. 27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent 10.1 retained juniors in service and also 
made fresh appointments after termination of her services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of 
the Act. Thus, there is violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4. Notice of the petition was given to respondents.

5. Respondent no.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to 
the Court with clean hands as she was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage 
rate as prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non- 
Cantonment Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering 
respondent entered into contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). 
In July 2018, the answering respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and M/s 
Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e-tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide conservancy 
services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for 
payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed their duties and answering respondent is only 
responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command Chandigarh to release payment directly to the 
contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is 
carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent has no responsibility of 
disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed 
union in the headquarter, which is not permitted and also carried out demonstration inside the premises of 
Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent asked 
respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility 
for termination services of the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the 
answering respondent and the workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the 
answering respondent cannot organize themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative 
office of the Government of India. In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union 
unauthorizedly and indulge in unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor 
and therefore, termination is the prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed. 


6. It is pertinent to mention here that respondent no.2 was proceeded ex parte on 07.05.2024. 


Evidence of workman:- 


7. In order to prove his case, workman examined himself as WW1 and tendered into evidence his affidavit 
WW/1/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent no.1. AR for workman closed the evidence on 
22.07.2024. 


Evidence of respondent no.1:- 


8. Respondent 10.1 examined Colonel K P Singh S/o Late Colonel P. P. Singh, OIC, Civic Cell, Station 
Head Quarter, Chandi Mandir Panchkula as MW1, who tendered into evidence his affidavit Ex. MW1/A along 
with documents Ex.R1 to Ex.R4. AR for respondent no.1 closed the evidence on 29.01.2026. 


Sr. No. Document Dated Exhibit 
1. Policy 18.03.2011 Ex.R-1 
2. Agreement with respondent no.2 05.07.2018 Ex.R-2 
3: Copy of ECR of EPFO Ex.R-3 
4 Letter of Head Quarter 22.04.1980 Ex.R-4 


Submissions of workman:- 


9. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by 
respondent 10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent 10.2. The workman was appointed directly by 
respondent 10.1 on 01.04.2017 as sweeper and her services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any 
reason in violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and 
junior to him were retained in service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So 
far as the agreements between the respondent 10.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair 
labour practice. The work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having 
any license. The contractor has left after three months. No domestic inquiry was held before terminating the 
service of the workman, which is mandatory under the Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 


10. On the other hand, AR for respondent no.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent 
10.2 (contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent 10.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no 
relationship of employer and employee between respondent 10.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by the 
respondent 10.2 to the workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating the 
services of the workman. Workman is employee of respondent no.2. If there is any violation of provision of 
the Act, then it is done by respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the contractor with regard to 
EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed union in the Headquarter, which is not 
permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent no.1 being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of

his appointment by respondent 10.2 and has filed a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the 
workman is not maintainable. 


11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 
12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing 
his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. She was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to 
perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 


Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are 
not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract 
basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be 
inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract 
basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in 
plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In 
view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein 
admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 


Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in 
the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, 
salary, letter of appointment by respondent no.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature 
for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally 
lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 Colonel K P 
Singh in his cross examination has stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the 
conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to 
the conservancy staff. Contractor is responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent 10.2 who 
was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. 
Ex.R-2 is the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges 
that workman was paid salary by the contractor and she was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. 
Thus, there does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 
10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was 
supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 


2316 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 4, 2026/CHAITRA 14, 1948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) 
of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. 
The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 
(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to 
calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in her deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G 
and 25H of the Act. She also stated that she was appointed on 01.04.2017 and she was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. She was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, she has further stated 
that her salary used to be credited in his bank account. But she has not placed on record any bank account, in 
which her salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. 
However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from 
the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis 
were provided by respondent 10.2 (contractor) to work with respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of 
respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed above. There does not exist any relationship 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of 
employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as 
regards violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the 
workman. Hence, workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by 
respondent 10.1 by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement 
executed between respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions 
of AR for workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry 
was held before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that 
workman was entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and 
no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not 
mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a 
department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is 
provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is not employee of 
respondent no.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent 10.2 (contractor) is currently not 
working with respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary 
given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, 
this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of 
compensation is deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


1. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


ii. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 


iii. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


24. Present workman employed on 01.04.2017 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (less than 2 years), so 
she is entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


25. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.20,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the 
date of award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent 10.1 requires safai 
karamcharis, then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground. 


26. Let copy of this award be sent to Central Government for publication as required under Section 17 
of the Act.

1. Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against her termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along 
with continuity of service and full back wages. 


2. It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that she was appointed as sweeper/safai 
karamchari on 16.03.2012 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But 
the said minimum wages were never paid to her. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 1.75% 
ESI and Rs.300/- as TDS from his salary despite of the fact that her total wages comes under the ambit of tax 
free limit. She was working under respondent no.1 directly, but respondent no.1 in order to avoid its liability 
always shows his employment in record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


3. It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent 10.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent 10.1. However, their demand was not 
accepted. Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently her services were 
dispensed with w.e.f. 27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent no.1 retained juniors in service and also 
made fresh appointments after termination of her services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of 
the Act. Thus, there is violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4. Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


5. Respondent no.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to the 
Court with clean hands as she was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage rate 
as prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non- 
Cantonment Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering 
respondent entered into contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). 
In July 2018, the answering respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and M/s 
Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e-tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide conservancy 
services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for 
payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed their duties and answering respondent is only responsible 
to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command Chandigarh to release payment directly to the contractor’s 
account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is carried out by the 
contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent has no responsibility of disbursement of wages and 
deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed union in the headquarter,

which is not permitted and also carried out demonstration inside the premises of Station Headquarter on 
27.10.2018 and failed to perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent asked respondent no.2 to ask the 
workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility for termination services of 
the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the answering respondent and the 
workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the answering respondent cannot

unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor and therefore, termination is the 
prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed. 


6. It is pertinent to mention here that respondent no.2 was proceeded ex parte on 07.05.2024.

WW/1/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent no.1. AR for workman closed the evidence on

8. Respondent 10.1 examined Colonel K P Singh S/o Late Colonel P. P. Singh, OIC, Civic Cell, Station Head 
Quarter, Chandi Mandir Panchkula as MW1, who tendered into evidence his affidavit Ex.MW1/A along with 
documents Ex.R1 to Ex.R4. AR for respondent 10.1 closed the evidence on 29.01.2026.

Submissions of workman:- 


9. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by 
respondent 10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent 10.2. The workman was appointed directly by 
respondent 10.1 on 16.03.2012 as sweeper and her services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any 
reason in violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and 
junior to him were retained in service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So 
far as the agreements between the respondent no.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair 
labour practice. The work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having 
any license. The contractor has left after three months. No domestic inquiry was held before terminating the 
service of the workman, which is mandatory under the Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 


10. On the other hand, AR for respondent no.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent no.2 
(contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent 10.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no 
relationship of employer and employee between respondent 10.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by the 
respondent 10.2 to the workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating the 
services of the workman. Workman is employee of respondent no.2. If there is any violation of provision of 
the Act, then it is done by respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the contractor with regard to 
EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed union in the Headquarter, which is not 
permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent 10.1 being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of 
his appointment by respondent 10.2 and has filed a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the 
workman is not maintainable. 


11. Ihave given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 


12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing 
his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. She was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to 
perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 


Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


[भाग त----खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/चैत्र 14, 1948 2331 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are 
not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract 
basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be 
inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract 
basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in 
plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In 
view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein 
admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. 
Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether 
the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the 
claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, 
letter of appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for 
holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking 
not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in 
his cross examination has stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the 
conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to 
the conservancy staff. Contractor is responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who 
was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent no.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 
is the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that 
workman was paid salary by the contractor and she was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. 
Thus, there does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 
10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying 
contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. 
Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) 


of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. 
The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 
(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to 
calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent 10.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in her deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 
25H of the Act. She also stated that she was appointed on 16.03.2012 and she was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. She was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, she has further stated 


2332 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 4, 2026/CHAITRA 14, 1948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


that her salary used to be credited in his bank account. But she has not placed on record any bank account, in 
which her salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. 
However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from 
the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis 
were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of 
respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.1 as has been discussed above. There does not exist any relationship 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of 
employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. 
Hence, workman is entitled for compensation from respondent 10.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent 
10.1 by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed 
between respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for 
workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held 
before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was 
entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic 
inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any 
right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of 
Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman 
cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being 
employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working 
with respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to 
him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this 
Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


i. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs. 20,000/-. 


ii. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 


iii. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs. 50,000/-. 


24. Present workman employed on 16.03.2012 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 5 years), so she 
is entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


25. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.50,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the 
date of award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent 10.1 requires safai 
karamcharis, then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground. 


26. Let copy of this award be sent to Central Government for publication as required under Section 17 of the 
Act.

1. Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against his termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along 
with continuity of service and full back wages. 


2. It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that he was appointed as sweeper/safai 
karamchari on 27.10.2014 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But 
the said minimum wages were never paid to him. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 
1.75% ESI and Rs.300/- as TDS from hissalary despite of the fact that his total wages comes under the ambit 
of taxfree limit. He was working under respondent no.1 directly, but respondent no.1 in order to avoid its 
liability always shows his employment in record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour 
practice. 


3६ It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent 10.1 raised 
the demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent 10.1. However, their demand was 
not accepted. Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently his services were 
dispensed with w.e.f. 27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent no.1 retained juniors in service and also 
made fresh appointments after termination of his services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of 
the Act. Thus, there is violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4. Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


5. Respondent no.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to 
the Court with clean hands as he was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage 
rate as prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non- 
Cantonment Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering 
respondent entered into contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). 
In July 2018, the answering respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and M/s 
Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e-tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide conservancy 
services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for 
payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed their duties and answering respondent is only 
responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command Chandigarh to release payment directly to the 
contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is 
carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent has no responsibility of 
disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed

basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be

inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing

distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in 
plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In

admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act.

out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:-

Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who 
was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time.

10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2.

supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor;

1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) 


of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. 
The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 
(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to 
calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry.

regards violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the

i. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-.

Rs.30,000/-.

executed between respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions 
of AR for workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry 
was held before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that 
workman was entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and 
no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not 
mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a 
department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is 
provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is not employee of 
respondent no.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor).

working with respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary 
given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, 
this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of 
compensation is deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


i. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


ii. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 


iii. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


24. Present workman employed on 01.01.2015 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 2 years 
and less than 5 years), so she is entitled for Rs.30,000/-.

carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent has no responsibility of 
disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed

Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent asked 
respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility 
for termination services of the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the 
answering respondent and the workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the 
answering respondent cannot organize themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative 
office of the Government of India. In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union

unauthorizedly and indulge in unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor

his appointment by respondent no.2 and has filed a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the 
workman is not maintainable. 


11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 


12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing 
his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to 
perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 


Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are 
not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract 
basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be 
inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing

whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract 
basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in 
plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In 
view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein 
admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 


Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in 
the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, 
salary, letter of appointment by respondent no.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature 
for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally 
lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P 
Singh in his cross examination has stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the 
conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to 
the conservancy staff. Contractor is responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who 
was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. 
Ex.R-2 is the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges 
that workman was paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. 
Thus, there does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 
10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was 
supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) 


of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. 
The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 
(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to 
calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G 
and 25H of the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 01.04.2017 and he was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated 
that his salary used to be credited in his bank account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in 
which his salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. 
However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from 
the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis 
were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of

respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.1 as has been discussed above. There does not exist any relationship 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of 
employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as 
regards violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the 
workman. Hence, workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by 
respondent 10.1 by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement 
executed between respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions 
of AR for workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry 
was held before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that 
workman was entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and 
no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not 
mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a 
department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is 
provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is not employee of 
respondent no.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not 
working with respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary 
given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, 
this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of 
compensation is deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


i. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


ii. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 


iii, Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


24. Present workman employed on 01.04.2017 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (less than 2 years), so 
he is entitled for Rs.20,000/-.

notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the

karamcharis, then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground.
